# Judges 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Song

Judges 5 is the “Song of Deborah,” one of the oldest extant poems in the Hebrew Bible. Ellicott calls it “one of the grandest outbursts of impassioned poetry in the Bible” and a victory ode (epinician) that surpasses even Pindar in “energy, scorn, and pathos” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Precept Austin notes that this is the only song recorded in the ~350 years covered by Judges, and that the verb “sang” is feminine singular — Deborah is the primary author and lead singer, with Barak joining her (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary). Nearly all commentators agree the song is authentic and contemporary with the events.

Gill’s Exposition outlines the song’s flow: the majestic appearance of God at Seir/Sinai (vv. 1–5), Israel’s miserable state before victory (vv. 6–8), a call to recount God’s righteous acts (vv. 9–11), praise for willing tribes and reproach for the negligent (vv. 14–18), the battle and curse on Meroz (vv. 19–23), commendation of Jael (vv. 24–27), the disappointed hope of Sisera’s mother (vv. 28–30), and concluding prayer (v. 31) (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).

---

## v. 1 — “On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song”

- **Deborah as sole composer.** Though both are named, the Hebrew verb “sang” is feminine singular, indicating Deborah was the author. Barak joined in singing, much as Miriam led the women while Moses led the men at the Red Sea (Exodus 15). Gill notes that Kimchi and Ben Gersom agree Deborah alone composed it (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm). Precept Austin says Barak “joined her in the victory celebration” just as he had joined her in battle (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).
- **“On that day.”** Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the song was sung immediately after the victory, showing “the priority of praise in believers’ lives.” Spurgeon is quoted: “Deborah sang concerning the overthrow of Israel’s enemies… we have a far richer theme for music; we have been delivered from worse enemies, and saved by a greater salvation” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- This is a song theologically parallel to the Song of Moses (Exodus 15) — both celebrate God’s supernatural overthrow of horses and chariots (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).

---

## v. 2 — “When the princes take the lead in Israel, when the people volunteer, bless the LORD”

- **Translation difficulty.** The Hebrew is obscure. Ellicott says the word *peraoth* (translated “princes” or “leaders”) may derive from “hair,” suggesting “long-haired ones” (nobles who wore long hair) or “hairy champions.” He renders it: “For the leading of the leaders of Israel, for the self-devotion of the people — praise ye the Lord” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). The ESV Study Bible (cited by Precept Austin) notes an alternative reading: “When locks of hair grow long in Israel,” possibly alluding to the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:5), connoting dedication to holy war (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).
- **Theme of willing leadership and followership.** Guzik explains: “Leadership is important in any endeavor and especially in the work of God… Leaders are nothing without followers, and it is the job of the people to willingly offer themselves.” He compares it to a conductor and orchestra — both must do their part (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **God’s sovereignty in human willingness.** Gill stresses that the people’s willingness “was owing to the secret influence of divine Providence on their hearts, moving and drawing them to this service; and therefore praise was due to the Lord” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- Precept Austin adds: The word “volunteered” (*nadab*) “connotes an uncompelled and free movement of the will unto divine service or sacrifice” (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).

---

## v. 3 — “Listen, O kings! Give ear, O princes! I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel”

- **Audience: Gentile kings.** Ellicott says the appeal is to “the kings of the earth” (as in Psalm 2:10), not Israelite rulers — Deborah wants all potentates to hear what God has done. Gill agrees: she desires “that all potentates might hear of the wonderful works of God… and be cautious how they oppressed the people of God” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm). The Targum restricts it to the kings allied with Jabin, but Gill finds that unlikely since they were probably slain.
- **Personal, intense praise.** The repetition “I, even I, will sing” expresses how “cordial, earnest, and vehement she was in her praise and thankfulness to God” (Gill). Guzik simply notes that Deborah sings directly to the Lord, not about Him — her worship is personal (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 4 — “O LORD, when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the land of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water”

- **What event is recalled?** Commentators differ. **Gill** and many older Jewish commentators see this as the giving of the Law at Sinai (referencing Deuteronomy 33:2). But **Ellicott** argues the mention of Seir and Edom points instead to Israel’s march from Kadesh Barnea toward Canaan, when God fought for them with earthquakes and storms — just as He now did against Sisera. He notes the events are “not recorded in the Pentateuch” but preserved in poetic memory (Psalm 68:7–9; Habakkuk 3:3–12) (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- **Connection to the present victory.** Guzik says: “God won the victory for Israel over Sisera by sending a great rain… In this song Deborah recalled a time when God did the same thing on behalf of Israel in the days of the Exodus.” The storm that swelled the Kishon (v. 21) mirrors God’s ancient march (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **Ligonier** (Reformed) notes the “supernatural intervention” of the storm: God “sent a storm to flood the Kishon River, giving the advantage to the Israelites” (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/deborah-barak).
- Precept Austin highlights that “the main theme of the song is ‘the righteous acts’ of the LORD Himself, who went forth as Israel’s champion and overwhelmed His enemies by unleashing the powers of heaven against them” (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).

---

## v. 5 — “The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel”

- **“The One of Sinai”** — Ellicott translates “even this Sinai,” as though Deborah “actually saw the sacred mountain before her.” He explains: “even as Sinai was moved (Psalm 68:8), so the mountains of Edom seemed to melt away before the march of Jehovah” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- **“Mountains melted”** — Gill: a figurative expression for the terror of the inhabitants; or literally what happened at Sinai, where the mountain quaked at God’s presence (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- Guzik: “It is good to remember that God’s goodness to His people didn’t just start today. He has been good to His people for a long, long time” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 6 — “In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were deserted and the travelers took the byways”

- **Why “in the days of Jael”?** Ellicott finds it remarkable that Jael is named as a contemporary of Shamgar — it shows that even the presence of heroic figures like Shamgar and Jael “was unavailing to deliver them until Deborah arose.” He rejects emendations to “Jair” or “the helper,” insisting Jael is the Kenite woman of chapter 4 and may have been a person of “great importance and influence” even before killing Sisera (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- **Condition of the land.** Gill: “the public roads were so infested with thieves and robbers… travellers and merchants… were obliged to go in private roads, and roundabout ways” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm). Guzik cites Adam Clarke: “The land was full of anarchy and confusion, being everywhere infested with banditti” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 7 — “Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel”

- **“Villages ceased” — translation issue.** The Hebrew *perāzôn* is difficult. Ellicott argues against “villages” and prefers “warlike chiefs” or “princes” (LXX: *dunatoi*, Vulgate: *fortes*). So: “Ceased the warriors in Israel, ceased, until I arose — Deborah” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Precept Austin notes the LXX renders it “The mighty men in Israel failed” (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary). However, Gill and Guzik retain the traditional “villages” sense: villagers fled to fortified cities for safety (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **“A mother in Israel.”** Gill says this expresses her “maternal affection” — she was a “nursing mother to Israel, to teach and instruct them in the mind and will of God, to administer judgement and justice… to protect and defend them” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm). Guzik says this wasn’t pride but recognition that “God works through willing individuals, and she was the willing one in this crisis” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **DesiringGod** (Reformed Baptist): Deborah is a model of a “word-filled woman” who speaks, obeys, and sings God’s word — “a ‘mother in Israel’… bearing witness to the ways God uses men and women to serve him” (desiringgod.org/articles/what-makes-a-woman-strong).

---

## v. 8 — “When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates. Not a shield or spear was found among forty thousand in Israel”

- **Idolatry as cause.** Ellicott says the Chaldee and LXX support “they chose new gods,” alluding to the idolatry that provoked God’s judgment (Deuteronomy 32:16–17). The Vulgate and Syriac read “God chose new things” (i.e., new wars), but Ellicott finds this “a poorer sense” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Gill also takes it as Israel’s idolatry: “when they fell into idolatry, then God suffered the judgment of war to come upon them” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- **“Not a shield or spear.”** Guzik says “Israel’s oppressors… confiscated all weapons, so the Israelites could not fight” — and draws a spiritual analogy: “Satan doesn’t only want to oppress the Christian; he also wants to disarm the believer” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/). Ellicott, however, thinks it means the Israelites were too cowed to *dare* put on armor, rather than being literally disarmed (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- Gill notes an intriguing alternative: some Jewish commentators (Ben Gersom) referred this to the Benjamite civil war where 40,000 Israelites fell (Judges 20:21), which predated Deborah (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).

---

## v. 9 — “My heart is with the princes of Israel, with the volunteers among the people. Bless the LORD!”

- **Refrain echoing v. 2.** Guzik notes: “In Judges 5:2, Deborah spoke of the people offering themselves willingly. Here she notes that the sacrifices should also be borne by the leaders. They also must offer themselves willingly.” He adds, “Deborah didn’t only care for her job of leadership. She also had a heart for other leaders and their work” — a sign of mature leadership (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **DesiringGod** emphasizes this verse: “My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the Lord” — showing Deborah’s heart for God’s ordained male leaders (desiringgod.org/articles/what-makes-a-woman-strong).
- Gill: Deborah’s heart was toward the “nobles and rulers” who “offered themselves willingly among the people… thereby setting a good example, and animating the people to battle” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).

---

## v. 10 — “You who ride white donkeys, who sit on saddle blankets, and you who travel the road, ponder”

- **Three classes addressed.** Ellicott explains Deborah appeals to (1) the wealthy riding “bright-coloured” (not literally white) donkeys, (2) those who sit on “rich divans” or “bright carpets,” and (3) ordinary foot-travellers — all are to “think of it” (i.e., meditate on the song) (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- **White donkeys as status symbols.** Gill provides extensive cultural detail: “white asses were the most valuable, and chiefly used by great personages” — citing that sons of judges rode on asses’ colts (Judges 10:4; 12:14) (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- Guzik: “The song asked the civic leaders along with Deborah and Barak to tell the villagers in Israel the great things God did” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 11 — “the voices of the singers at the watering places. There they shall recount the righteous acts of the LORD…”

- **“At the watering places.”** Ellicott acknowledges the Hebrew is “highly uncertain.” The traditional KJV reading (“They that are delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water”) is “a conjectural addition.” The imagery is of women and shepherds now able to gather safely at wells, free from enemy archers, and there they sing of God’s righteous acts (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Gill: “coming to those places again, it would put them in mind to what hazards and dangers they had been exposed formerly… and this would lead them to discourse of and repeat the righteous dealings of God” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- **“Then the people of the LORD went down to the gates.”** Gill explains: they can now freely go to “the gates of their own cities” — resuming normal life, including courts of justice held at the city gates, without fear (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- **Spurgeon** preached a sermon on this verse (cited by Precept Austin), spiritualizing it: “Those who went to draw water at the wells after Barak’s victory, were no longer disturbed by the robbers who lurked at the fountains… instead of drawing the water by stealth and in hasty fear, the women joined their voices around the well head, and sang” — a picture of Christian liberty and security in Christ (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_notes).

---

## v. 12 — “‘Awake, awake, O Deborah! Awake, awake, sing a song! Arise, O Barak, and take hold of your captives, O son of Abinoam!’”

- **Self-exhortation.** Deborah rouses herself — a “new prelude” (Ellicott) marking the transition to the muster and battle section. Gill: “Either perceiving some languor and remissness in her spirits… or rather finding herself more impressed with a sense of the great and good things the Lord had done… calls upon her soul to exert all its powers” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).
- **“Lead thy captivity captive.”** Ellicott renders it “lead in triumph thy long train of captives.” He notes this language is echoed in Revelation 13:10 and applied messianically. Guzik: “Believers should never hide our light under a bushel… Many need to wake up and sing a song of praise” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 13 — “Then the survivors came down to the nobles; the people of the LORD came down to me against the mighty”

- **A “remnant” goes to battle.** Ellicott: “Then descended a remnant of the nobles of the people.” They were only “a remnant” because at least six tribes held aloof. He renders: “Jehovah descended to me among the heroes” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- Guzik: “As she remembered God’s help, Deborah knew that His help came from the tribes of Israel, stirred to join in the battle” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## vv. 14–15a — The Loyal Tribes

- **Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (West Manasseh), Zebulun, Issachar.** Ellicott explains each: “Out of Ephraim (came) those whose root is in Amalek” — Ephraim had firmly rooted itself in territory once held by Amalekites. “After thee, Benjamin” — Benjamin followed Ephraim’s lead, a war-cry echoed in Hosea 5:8. “Out of Machir came masters” — Machir represents the western half of Manasseh (the eastern half apparently stayed home). “From Zebulon chieftains, with the marshal’s staff” — military commanders. “The princes of Issachar, with Deborah” — they rushed into the valley (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- Guzik notes the silence regarding Judah and Simeon is striking — these southern tribes are not mentioned (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- Gill notes Issachar “rushed into the valley at his heels” on foot against 900 iron chariots — “a mark of extraordinary valour” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).

---

## vv. 15b–17 — The Tribes That Did Not Help

### Reuben (vv. 15b–16)
- **“Great indecision” / “great resolves of heart.”** The Hebrew can mean either. Ellicott renders: “By the streams of Reuben was courage of word… By the streams of Reuben was cowardice in deed.” The Reubenites talked bravely but stayed home listening to shepherds’ flutes (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Guzik: the repetition “shows the singer’s frustration — they talked about it, but did nothing” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

### Gilead (v. 17a)
- **East Manasseh and Gad.** “Gilead remained beyond the Jordan” — the Transjordanian tribes stayed home. Ellicott: “Gilead beyond Jordan lingered” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).

### Dan (v. 17b)
- **“Why did you linger by the ships?”** Dan’s territory included a coastal region; they were occupied with maritime commerce and did not join. Guzik notes this as a reproach (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

### Asher (v. 17c)
- **“Asher stayed at the coast and remained in his harbors.”** Similar to Dan — secure in their coastal strongholds, they refused to help.

Guzik summarizes: “Reuben, East Manasseh, Dan, and Asher did not join in the battle.” Trapp (cited by Guzik): “All these are worthily shamed and shented, though they were not without some sorry pleas and pretences” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 18 — “Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield”

- **Highest praise for the bravest.** Ellicott: “Zebulon — a people flinging its soul to death! And Naphtali — on the heights of the field.” These two tribes bore the brunt of the fighting. Guzik contrasts them with the stay-at-home tribes: “The song contrasts the tribes that jeopardized their lives in the battle… with those who sat it out… showing how we’re defined by who stands with God and who doesn’t” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 19 — “Kings came and fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, but they took no plunder of silver”

- **Location.** Taanach and Megiddo are in the Jezreel Valley, a strategic plain ideal for chariot warfare — which makes the Canaanite defeat all the more remarkable.
- **“Took no plunder of silver.”** Ellicott: “No dust of silver did they win” — they expected to enrich themselves by plundering Israel but gained nothing. Guzik: “Instead of gaining plunder, the kings of Canaan were themselves plundered” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## v. 20 — “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera”

- **Divine intervention, not astrology.** All commentators agree this is poetic language for God fighting from heaven through a providential storm — not literal stars or astral deities. Guzik: “The battle was fought from the heavens in the sense that God sent rain that made the Canaanite chariots of no use” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/). Ellicott: “From heaven they fought; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera” — the storm is personified as heavenly forces (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- Precept Austin links this to the broader biblical theme of God as divine warrior fighting for His people (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).

---

## v. 21 — “The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river, the River Kishon. March on, O my soul, in strength!”

- **The Kishon as God’s weapon.** Ellicott: “The torrent Kishon swept them away; the torrent of slaughters, the torrent Kishon.” A sudden storm turned the normally placid Kishon into a raging flood that bogged down and swept away the iron chariots. Guzik: the river is called “ancient” perhaps to emphasize that “God used a weapon that was always there, but now employed by Him for His purposes” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **“March on, O my soul, in strength!”** A personal exhortation to press forward. Ellicott renders: “Trample, my soul, on strength!” — a cry of triumph over the defeated enemy.

---

## v. 22 — “Then the hooves of horses thundered— the mad galloping of his stallions”

- **The rout.** Ellicott’s vivid rendering: “Then stamped the hoofs of the steeds with the plungings, the plungings of the mighty ones!” The poetry evokes the panic of Sisera’s chariot horses fleeing in terror from the flood (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).

---

## v. 23 — “‘Curse Meroz,’ says the angel of the LORD. ‘Bitterly curse her inhabitants; for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty’”

- **Who or what is Meroz?** The location is unknown. Ellicott suggests it was a village on Sisera’s flight path that failed to apprehend him (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Dr. Constable (cited in studylight.org) proposes it may be Merom in Naphtali, west of Hazor — Israelites who feared reprisals and did nothing.
- **Neutrality is hostility.** **Smith’s Bible Commentary** (on StudyLight) makes the application: “The curse of Meroz was the curse of not doing anything, trying to take a neutral position, standing back and not offering to help in the work of God. It is tragic that many people today are guilty of the same thing” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/judges-5.html). Guzik: “God still accomplished His work, but the city of Meroz was cursed because they had no part in it” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **“The angel of the LORD.”** A divine messenger pronounces the curse, giving it ultimate authority. Gill takes it as the pre-incarnate Christ or a theophanic angel (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).

---

## v. 24 — “Most blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women”

- **Jael contrasted with Meroz.** Ellicott notes: “With the selfish indifference of the men of Meroz she contrasts the valorous enthusiasm of Jael the Kenite.” The blessing on Jael is as emphatic as the curse on Meroz (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- **“Most blessed among women.”** This language echoes later messianic blessing (Luke 1:42: “Blessed are you among women”). Constable (cited in studylight.org) says Jael is “the embodiment of God’s will for justice and righteousness” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-5.html).
- **Ligonier** (Reformed) titles the section “The Glory of Jael” and sees her as an instrument of God’s judgment despite her unconventional method (learn.ligonier.org/scripture/judges-5).

---

## v. 25 — “He asked for water, and she gave him milk. In a magnificent bowl she brought him curds”

- **Hospitality used as strategy.** Ellicott notes that Jael gave him rich curds in “a bowl of the nobles,” lulling Sisera into a false sense of security and deepening his sleep (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Gill: “curds” refers to “the coagulated part of milk from which cheese comes, in contrast to the watery whey” — a rich, sleep-inducing drink (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/5.htm).

---

## v. 26 — “She reached for the tent peg, her right hand for the workman’s hammer. She struck Sisera and crushed his skull; she shattered and pierced his temple”

- **Graphic detail.** Ellicott: “And she hammered Sisera, shattered his head, and battered and crashed through his temples.” The vivid, repetitive language heightens the drama. Guzik notes the word “pounded” reflects repeated, violent blows (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **Ethical question.** Guzik raises the tension: “The responsibility to protect and bless a guest was an almost absolute command, and Jael killed a guest. Yet she was blessed here because her obedience to the cause of God was greater than her obedience to tradition and custom” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/). Constable likewise: “The greatest argument for the propriety of Jael’s action is God’s honoring of her in this song” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-5.html).

---

## v. 27 — “At her feet he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still; at her feet he collapsed, he fell; where he collapsed, there he fell dead”

- **Repetition for emphasis and mockery.** Ellicott’s translation captures the rhythm: “Between her feet he writhed, he fell, he lay; between her feet he writhed, he fell; where he writhed there he fell down — dead!” Guzik says Deborah “wanted to increase Sisera’s shame by pointing out that it was a woman who ended his life.” Poole (cited by Guzik): “At the first blow or wound he was awakened, and made some attempt to rise; but… he found himself impotent, and fell down dead” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

---

## vv. 28–30 — The Mother of Sisera

### v. 28 — “Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented…”

- **Dramatic irony.** The scene shifts to Sisera’s home, where his mother waits anxiously. Ellicott: “Through the window looked forth and wailed the mother of Sisera… ‘Why lingers his chariot to come? Why tarry the pacings of his chariots?’” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html). Guzik: “Every death has consequences and Deborah thought of and celebrated the consequences of Sisera’s death” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

### vv. 29–30 — “Her wisest ladies answer; indeed she keeps telling herself, ‘Are they not finding and dividing the spoil…’”

- **Self-deception.** The mother and her ladies imagine Sisera is delayed by the abundance of plunder — including captive women. Ellicott: “The wise of her princesses answer her; yea, she repeats their words to herself.” They imagine “a maiden, two maidens, to each man,” dyed and embroidered garments for Sisera (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- **“A girl or two for each warrior.”** Guzik notes the Hebrew word (*raḥam*) is crude — “Elsewhere in the Old Testament it means ‘womb’… The nearest English equivalent is ‘wench’” (Cundall, cited in enduringword.com). This exposes the brutal contempt the Canaanites held for defeated women.
- **Grim irony.** The mother’s imaginings of victory and plunder contrast devastatingly with the reality: Sisera lies dead under a woman’s tent peg.

---

## v. 31 — “So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest.” And the land had rest for forty years.

- **Imprecatory conclusion.** Ellicott: “So perish thine enemies, O Lord! But let those who love Thee be as the sun’s rising in his strength.” Guzik: “To love God is to hate His enemies. A man or woman is defined as much by who their enemies are as by who their friends are” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **Those who love Him shine.** Guzik: “How much better it is to be one of those who love Him than to be one of God’s enemies!” He adds, “we become like what we love and serve” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).
- **“The land had rest for forty years.”** A full generation of peace. Guzik ties this back to the song’s theme — when leaders lead and people volunteer, God grants rest. Precept Austin notes this is the longest period of rest recorded in Judges, showing the decisive nature of this victory (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).
- **Constable** makes the concluding application: “This verse invites the reader to consider how we too may join God in His work of crushing oppressors, His enemies, and so take our place among His friends” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-5.html).

## Denominational & Tradition-Specific Notes

### Reformed (Ligonier)
- Emphasizes God’s **sovereign intervention** through the storm as a supernatural act (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/deborah-barak).
- Sees Barak’s reluctance (from ch. 4) as evidence of imperfect faith: “God can use people even when their faith is less than perfect, but we lose out on blessings when we doubt His promises.”
- Deborah’s role as prophetess is seen in light of the **failure of the priesthood** at the time: “Ordinarily, the people were to go to the priests for judgment (Deut. 17:8–13), but in the era of the judges, so many priests were spiritually unqualified that their counsel was not sought.”

### Reformed Baptist (DesiringGod / John Piper)
- Deborah is celebrated as a “**word-filled woman**” who speaks, obeys, and sings God’s word — a model for women today.
- Emphasis on **complementarian leadership**: “My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel” (v. 9) shows Deborah’s heart for God’s ordained male leaders. “I pray for my heart to go out to the men God calls as spiritual leaders of the church.”
- The article stresses that Deborah did not exercise military leadership — she called Barak to do so — and that she “revels in the blessing of both women and men offering themselves willingly to the Lord, to do the distinct jobs he calls them to do” (desiringgod.org/articles/what-makes-a-woman-strong).

### Baptist / Spurgeon
- **Spurgeon** (cited throughout by Guzik and Precept Austin) read the song Christologically: “We have a far richer theme for music; we have been delivered from worse enemies, and saved by a greater salvation.”
- On v. 11, Spurgeon spiritualized the watering places: the believer now draws water (the Word, the Spirit) without fear, joining with others to sing of God’s righteous acts (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_notes).
- Spurgeon also cited Luther’s practice: “When he had been most slandered… Luther would gather together his friends, and say, ‘Come let us sing a psalm and spite the devil’” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-5/).

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik)
- Guzik’s commentary is used broadly but is associated with Calvary Chapel / charismatic evangelicalism. Distinctives include:
  - **Spiritual warfare analogy**: “Satan doesn’t only want to oppress the Christian; he also wants to disarm the believer” (on v. 8).
  - Emphasis on **willingness and volunteerism** as Spirit-led response.
  - **Application-focused**: each section ends with practical takeaways about leadership, courage, and praise.

### Older / Traditional Commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit)
- **Gill** (18th-century Baptist) provides extensive Jewish interpretive tradition (Kimchi, Ben Gersom, Targum) alongside literal exegesis.
- **Ellicott** (19th-century Anglican) focuses on the Hebrew text, poetic structure, and ancient Near Eastern context. He defends the poem’s early date and authenticity.
- **The Pulpit Commentary** (cited through StudyLight excerpts) emphasizes the poem’s “wonderful beauty and lyric power” and notes that the verb “sang” is feminine — Deborah was the composer.

### Modern Scholarship (noted in passing)
- Ellicott mentions that some scholars attempted to date the song late “because it contains certain forms which are asserted to be of late occurrence,” but notes it is “now generally admitted that these may be provincial or colloquial usages of great antiquity” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-5.html).
- Precept Austin explicitly **warns against allegorization** (citing Origen, who interpreted Deborah as a “bee” with “honey-sweet prophecies” and Jael as the Gentile church killing the devil), urging readers to follow literal, grammatical-historical hermeneutics (preceptaustin.org/judges_5_commentary).

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Common Reading |
|---|---|
| **God as Divine Warrior** | The storm, flood, and "stars fighting" are God's supernatural intervention — not human might (all traditions) |
| **Praise for obedience** | Jael is blessed despite violating hospitality customs, because loyalty to God surpasses cultural norms |
| **Willingness** | Both leaders and followers must offer themselves freely; the song praises volunteers and rebukes the hesitant |
| **Neutrality condemned** | Meroz is cursed for not helping, teaching that neutrality toward God's cause is effectively opposition |
| **Deborah's role** | She is the song's author, a prophetess, "a mother in Israel" — Reformed traditions stress she did not replace male military leadership; charismatic/evangelical readings emphasize her as a model of Spirit-led courage |
| **The fate of God's enemies vs. His lovers** | The closing verse (v. 31) frames the whole song as a picture of final judgment and reward |
